{{Short description|Theorem in probability theory}}

The '''Yamada–Watanabe theorem''' is a result from [[probability theory]] saying that for a large class of [[stochastic differential equation]]s a ''weak solution'' with ''pathwise uniqueness'' implies a ''strong solution'' and ''uniqueness in distribution''. In its original form, the theorem was stated for <math>n</math>-dimensional ''Itô equations'' and was proven by [[Toshio Yamada (mathematician)|Toshio Yamada]] and [[Shinzo Watanabe]] in 1971.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Toshio |last1=Yamada |first2=Shinzō |last2=Watanabe |title=On the uniqueness of solutions of stochastic differential equations |journal=J. Math. Kyoto Univ. |volume=11 |number=1 |pages=155 - 167 |date=1971 |doi=10.1215/kjm/1250523691}}</ref> Since then, many generalizations appeared particularly one for general [[semimartingale]]s by [[Jean Jacod]] from 1980.<ref name="Jacod">{{cite journal |first=Jean |last=Jacod |date=1980 |title=Weak and Strong Solutions of Stochastic Differential Equations |journal=Stochastics |volume=3 |pages=171-191 |doi=10.1080/17442508008833143}}</ref>

== Yamada–Watanabe theorem ==
=== History, generalizations and related results ===
[[Jean Jacod]] generalized the result to SDEs of the form
:<math>dX_t=u(X,Z)dZ_t,</math>
where <math>(Z_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> is a [[semimartingale]] and the coefficient <math>u</math> can depend on the path of <math>Z</math>.<ref name="Jacod" />

Further generalisations were done by Hans-Jürgen Engelbert (1991<ref name="Engelbert">{{cite journal |first=Hans-Jürgen |last=Engelbert |date=1991 |title=On the theorem of T. Yamada and S. Watanabe |journal=Stochastics and Stochastic Reports |volume=36 |number=3-4 |pages=205-216 |doi=10.1080/17442509108833718}}</ref>) and [[Thomas G. Kurtz]] (2007<ref>{{cite journal |first=Thomas G. |last=Kurtz |title=The Yamada-Watanabe-Engelbert theorem for general stochastic equations and inequalities |journal=Electron. J. Probab. |volume=12 |pages=951 - 965 |date=2007 |doi=10.1214/EJP.v12-431|doi-access=free }}</ref>). For SDEs in [[Banach space]]s there is a result from Martin Ondrejat (2004<ref>{{cite journal |first=Martin |last=Ondreját |title=Uniqueness for stochastic evolution equations in Banach spaces |journal=Dissertationes Math. (Rozprawy Mat.) |date=2004 |volume=426 |pages=1-63}}</ref>), one by [[Michael Röckner]], Byron Schmuland and Xicheng Zhang (2008<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Michael |last1=Röckner |first2=Byron |last2=Schmuland |first3=Xicheng |last3=Zhang |date=2008 |title=Yamada–Watanabe theorem for stochastic evolution equations in infinite dimensions |journal=Condensed Matter Physics |volume=11 |number=2 |pages=247–259}}</ref>) and one by Stefan Tappe (2013<ref>{{citation |date=2013 |first=Stefan |journal=Electronic Communications in Probability |last=Tappe |number=24 |pages=1–13 |title=The Yamada–Watanabe theorem for mild solutions to stochastic partial differential equations |volume=18}}<!-- auto-translated from German by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>).

The converse of the theorem is also true and called the ''dual Yamada–Watanabe theorem''. The first version of this theorem was proven by Engelbert (1991<ref name="Engelbert" />) and a more general version by Alexander Cherny (2002<ref name="Cherny">{{cite journal |doi=10.1137/S0040585X97979093 |first=Alexander S. |last=Cherny |title=On the Uniqueness in Law and the Pathwise Uniqueness for Stochastic Differential Equations |journal=Theory of Probability & Its Applications |volume=46 |number=3 |pages=406-419 |date=2002}}</ref>).

=== Setting ===
Let <math>n,r\in\mathbb{N}</math> and <math>C(\R_+,\R^n)</math> be the space of continuous functions. Consider the <math>n</math>-dimensional Itô equation
:<math>dX_t=b(t,X)dt+\sigma(t,X)dW_t,\quad X_0=x_0</math>
where
*<math>b\colon \R_+\times C(\R_+,\R^n)\to\R^n</math> and <math>\sigma \colon \R_+\times C(\R_+,\R^n)\to\R^{n\times r}</math> are [[predictable process]]es,
*<math>(W_t)_{t\geq 0}=\left((W^{(1)}_t,\dots,W^{(r)}_t)\right)_{t\geq 0}</math> is an <math>r</math>-dimensional [[Brownian Motion]],
*<math>x_0\in \R^n</math> is deterministic.

=== Basic terminology ===
We say ''uniqueness in distribution'' (or ''weak uniqueness''), if for two arbitrary solutions <math>(X^{(1)},W^{(1)})</math> and <math>(X^{(2)},W^{(2)})</math> defined on (possibly different) [[Filtration (probability theory)|filtered]] probability spaces  <math>(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1,\mathbf{F}_1,P_1)</math> and <math>(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2,\mathbf{F}_2,P_2)</math>, we have for their distributions <math>P_{X^{(1)}}=P_{X^{(2)}}</math>, where <math>P_{X^{(1)}}:=\operatorname{Law}(X_t^{1},t\geq 0)</math>.

We say ''pathwise uniqueness''  (or ''strong uniqueness'') if any two solutions <math>(X^{(1)},W)</math> and <math>(X^{(2)},W)</math>, defined on the same filtered probability spaces <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbf{F},P)</math> with the same <math>\mathbf{F}</math>-Brownian motion, are [[Stochastic process#Indistinguishable|indistinguishable]] processes, i.e. we have <math>P</math>-almost surely that <math>\{X_t^{(1)}=X_t^{(2)},t\geq 0\}</math>

=== Theorem ===
Assume the described setting above is valid, then the theorem is:
: If there is ''pathwise uniqueness'', then there is also ''uniqueness in distribution''. And if for every initial distribution, there exists a weak solution, then for every initial distribution, also a pathwise unique strong solution exists.<ref name="Engelbert" /><ref name="Cherny" />

Jacod's result improved the statement with the additional statement that
: If a weak solutions exists and pathwise uniqueness holds, then this solution is also a strong solution.<ref name="Jacod" />
